description: Team ATLAS 00 is an aerospace software and systems engineering team competing in the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Combining agency-grade flight rigor with next-generation autonomous computing, ATLAS 00 focuses on solving one of interplanetary travel's hardest problems: precision planetary touchdown.
summary:
Atlas00 introduces L.I.N.K. (Lunar Intelligence & Navigation Kit), a dynamic survival and navigation dashboard designed for unpredictable lunar missions. When launch schedules are delayed, static landing plans fail, risking total solar power loss and communication blackouts at the lunar south pole. L.I.N.K. solves this by pulling real-time ephemeris data from the NASA JPL Horizons API. It empowers mission planners to scrub through time, instantly visualizing how sunlight and Earth line-of-sight shift minute-by-minute over the Shackleton Crater.

Beyond planning, L.I.N.K. is an active survival system. If an anomaly like a solar eclipse occurs, our AI digital twin runs thousands of background simulations to autonomously reroute the lander to an illuminated safe zone. By conceptualizing regenerative thermal loops and orbital relays, we guarantee zero seconds of silence and 100% trajectory confidence. L.I.N.K. transforms hours of orbital mechanics into a single, intuitive interface securing the future of Artemis.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

L.I.N.K. is a dynamic mission-planning dashboard and autonomous survival system designed for lunar descents. Instead of forcing mission planners to read raw datasets, aerospace architects can use our visual time-slider to instantly observe how shadows and Earth visibility shift minute-by-minute over the lunar surface. The system guides the user through a cohesive five-step workflow—Dock at a conceptual Moon Station, Analyze light and communication data, Compare sites, receive a data-backed Recommendation, and Simulate the descent trajectory. To ensure accuracy, L.I.N.K. actively queries the NASA JPL Horizons API to calculate the exact elevation and azimuth angles of the Sun and Earth relative to specific lunar coordinates at any given UTC time.

What benefits does it have and what is the intended impact?

Our system transforms hours of manual orbital mechanics and ephemeris calculations into an instant, visually driven decision-making process. If a primary landing zone is compromised by an unpredicted eclipse or a launch delay, the system initiates automated contingency protocols to dynamically reroute the lander to the nearest safe, sun-illuminated alternative. The ultimate impact of this project is to eliminate critical points of failure during Artemis missions at the Lunar South Pole, specifically around extreme environments like the Shackleton Crater. By guaranteeing visual clarity for descent windows and theoretical zero-second communication blackouts via orbital relays, L.I.N.K. shifts the focus from simply planning a landing to actively securing astronaut survival during deep-space anomalies.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

To develop this project, we utilized the NASA JPL Horizons API to acquire precise Ephemeris data for Sun and Earth positioning. The user interface and presentation architecture were designed using Canva, Adobe Photoshop, and Adobe Lightroom. For our cinematic mission simulation.. The tension-driven audio and sound design for the simulation were engineered using BandLab, Audacity, and AI audio tools. The entire project was developed and rendered across high-performance custom Windows 11 desktops

How is your project creative and what factors did your team consider?

Rather than building a standard mathematical calculator, we creatively engineered an autonomous survival system wrapped in an immersive astronaut experience. We introduced the "Eclipse Protocol" scenario to demonstrate how our AI handles total power failure by rerouting the lander in milliseconds. To survive this reroute, we proposed "Regenerative Thermal Loops" that recycle waste heat from the thrusters to prevent the hull from freezing in -130°C lunar shadows, along with "Orbital Laser Relays" that bounce Earth signals off the Moon Space Station to prevent communication blackouts. While designing these innovations, our team carefully considered the profound topographical shadows cast by crater rims due to the low sun angle at the Lunar South Pole. We also factored in the dangers of razor-sharp regolith blast zones damaging nearby infrastructure, and the critical Earth-to-Moon communication latency that makes human reaction times too slow, thereby necessitating our autonomous AI rerouting logic.
